title: Star Cluster IC 348 (NIRCam image)
caption: The central part of the star cluster IC 348, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
celestial: IC 348 · constellation Perseus · about 1000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, and K. Luhman (Penn State University) and C. Alves de Oliveira (European Space Agency)

recognition.text: Ranked #85 on ESA/Webb’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Fine, hair-like pink-purple filaments fill the middle of this image, curving to either side of the center. On the right they form a prominent loop that seems to reach toward the viewer, while yellowish filaments sit at lower left. Two bright stars near the center show Webb's eight-point spikes. This is the heart of IC 348, a star cluster.

The wispy curtains are a reflection nebula, interstellar material bouncing back the light of the cluster's stars. It also contains carbon-bearing molecules called PAHs. The bright star closest to the center is really a pair of type B stars, the most massive in the cluster, and their winds may help shape the large loop.

Astronomers searched IC 348 for free-floating brown dwarfs, bodies with too little mass to be stars but bigger than most planets. They found three with less than eight times Jupiter's mass. The smallest weighs only three to four times as much as Jupiter, which challenges theories of how stars form.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.97 x 5.32 arcminutes) and distance (1000 light years), the frame spans roughly 1.2 × 1.5 light-years. Its light set out about 1,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This is a near-infrared image from Webb's NIRCam using three filters, with the shortest wavelength shown in blue, the middle in green and the longest in red.
understand.eye: This near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the faint brown dwarfs would be far too dim to see without a large telescope.
